text: Design a class that finds the kth largest element in a stream. The constructor gets k and a starting array, nums. Then add of val adds one number to the stream and returns the kth largest so far. It's kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct value.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — numbers only come in, and nothing is ever removed. After each add, if I sorted everything from big to small, I'd return the item at index k minus one. Duplicates count separately. Is that right?

Then here's the key thing I notice. To answer the kth largest, I never need the small numbers — only the top k. And out of those k, the answer is the smallest one. A number that falls below the top k can never matter again, because numbers only get added, so the top k can only get bigger. Are there any constraints on the input size?

nums has up to ten to the fourth numbers, and it can be empty. k is at least one and at most the length of nums plus one. Values are between minus ten to the fourth and ten to the fourth. And there are at most ten to the fourth calls to add.

Got it. The k at most length plus one part is important. It means after the first add, there are always at least k numbers, so the kth largest always exists when add returns. Let me run through the example: k is three, nums is four, five, eight, two. The top three are eight, five, four, so the answer starts at four. The answer only moves when a new number beats the smallest of the top three — that's the five and the nine. So adds of three, five, ten, nine, four give four, five, five, eight, eight, which matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to keep every number, and on each add, sort from big to small and take index k minus one. It's correct, but each call sorts up to twenty thousand numbers — with ten to the fourth nums and ten to the fourth adds, that takes about one point one seconds. Too slow. This problem reminds me of top-k selection with a bounded min-heap. The heap holds the k largest numbers seen so far, and its top is the smallest of them — exactly the kth largest. It sounds backwards to use a min-heap to find a largest element. But the top is a gatekeeper: any new number smaller than it can't be in the top k, so it gets kicked out right away.

Here's the plan. One: keep a min-heap, and store k for add. Two: in the constructor and in add, push the number, and if the heap grows past k, pop the smallest. Three: add returns the top. One thing worth flagging — push first, then pop. Pushing first lets the new number compete fairly; popping first throws away an old number before I even look at the new one. With k of one and adds of two then one, pop-first returns two, one, but the right answer is two, two. The constructor must trim too: with k of one, nums one, one, and add two, the untrimmed version returns one instead of two. A sorted list would shift elements, linear per add; the heap is log k per add, order k memory. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The greater-int comparator turns the priority queue into a min-heap — by default, C++ gives a max-heap. The constructor and add share the same step: push, then pop if the heap is bigger than k. Then add returns the top. One thing worth flagging — top on an empty heap is undefined behavior, so the heap must never be empty there. After the constructor, the size is the smaller of the nums length and k, so at least k minus one. The first add brings it to exactly k, and it stays k from then on. Since k is at least one, the top always exists.

Let's dry-run the code. k is three, nums is four, five, eight, two, then adds of three, five, ten, nine, four — expected null, four, five, five, eight, eight. The row that matters is add five: the new five beats the gatekeeper four, so four gets popped and the top becomes five. Nine does the same later, lifting the top to eight. Every other add pops the new number, or an equal five. That matches. Corner cases: k of one, empty nums, adds one then two give one, two — a max-heap by mistake gives one, one. k of two, nums one, add two returns one; an only-push-if-bigger-than-top shortcut wrongly returns two. Greater-or-equal in the pop check empties the heap when k is one, so top crashes.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is order n plus q, times log k, where n is the length of nums and q is the number of add calls. Each number is pushed once and popped at most once, and each heap operation is log k. Space is order k; the heap never holds more than k plus one numbers. In the worst case, with ten to the fourth nums, ten to the fourth adds and k of five thousand, the heap takes about point nine milliseconds, versus about one point one seconds for sort-every-add. Oh, one more thing — reading the answer is constant time, so if a system asked for the kth largest far more often than it added numbers, this design already fits.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that only the top k numbers matter, and that the answer is the smallest of them — which is why a min-heap is the right tool. You explained why the order is push, then pop, and why the constructor must trim, each with a tiny counterexample. And you used k at most length plus one to prove top never runs on an empty heap. Good work.
